subject: Science
title: Variations, Heredity and Cell Division
learningOutcomes: Define variation and distinguish between continuous, discontinuous and acquired variation.
Explain how organisms are adapted to their environment and how a variation becomes an adaptation.
Describe heredity, genes and alleles, and dominant versus recessive characteristics.
Describe the structure of DNA — the double helix, nucleotides and the four bases.
Compare mitosis and meiosis and put the stages of cell division in the correct order.

sections.heading: Variation Within a Species
sections.body: All human beings belong to one species, Homo sapiens. Members of the same species share the same general features but show small differences called variations. These differences exist because we inherit characteristics from both parents — some from the mother and some from the father. Variation is important because it has helped species survive and evolve over millions of years.

sections.heading: Types of Variation
sections.body: Continuous variation shows a smooth range of values between two limits, such as height and weight, and produces a bell-shaped normal distribution curve. Discontinuous variation falls into clear separate categories with no in-between, such as tongue rolling and eye colour. Acquired variation is not inherited — it develops during a lifetime because of the environment or what an organism does, such as a suntan or the effect of diet on weight.

sections.heading: Adaptation and Natural Selection
sections.body: An adaptation is a physical or behavioural feature that makes an organism better suited to its environment. The polar bear has blubber, small ears, white fur and big feet for arctic life; the cactus and camel have features that save water in the desert. An adaptation is more than a variation: it is a variation that has been selected because it gives a clear survival advantage. When a beneficial variation helps individuals survive and reproduce, it spreads over generations until the whole species has it — this process is natural selection.

sections.heading: Heredity, Genes and Alleles
sections.body: Heredity is the passing of characteristics from parents to offspring. Genetics, founded by Gregor Mendel using garden peas, is the study of how heredity works. Genes are the basic units of heredity; they are made of DNA and sit on chromosomes inside the nucleus. Alleles are different forms of the same gene. A dominant allele shows its effect even with one copy, while a recessive allele only shows when no dominant allele is present. An organism with two identical alleles (BB or bb) is homozygous; with two different alleles (Bb) it is heterozygous.

sections.heading: DNA
sections.body: DNA stands for deoxyribonucleic acid. It is shaped like a twisted ladder called a double helix. The sides of the ladder are made of deoxyribose sugar and phosphate groups, and the rungs are pairs of organic bases: Adenine (A), Thymine (T), Cytosine (C) and Guanine (G). A always pairs with T and C always pairs with G. The building block of DNA is the nucleotide, made of a sugar, a phosphate group and a base. About 99.9% of the DNA of every human is the same.

sections.heading: Cell Division: Mitosis and Meiosis
sections.body: Living things make new cells to grow, to replace dead cells and to make gametes. Mitosis produces two identical daughter cells for growth and repair; the cell first copies its DNA during interphase, then divides through prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase. Meiosis produces four gametes, each with half the chromosome number (haploid, n), so that when two gametes fuse at fertilisation the zygote has the full number (diploid, 2n). A mutation is a change in the DNA — the original source of all new variation.

definitions.definition: The small differences between individual members of the same species.
A physical or behavioural feature that helps an organism survive in its environment.
The process by which organisms with beneficial variations survive and reproduce more successfully, so the feature spreads.
A unit of hereditary information on a chromosome that controls one or more characteristics.
A different form of the same gene, e.g. a black-hair allele and a blond-hair allele.
Deoxyribonucleic acid — the chemical that makes up genes and chromosomes, shaped as a double helix.
Cell division that produces two identical daughter cells, used for growth and repair.
Cell division that produces four gametes, each with half the chromosome number.

examTips: FBISE questions often ask you to put the four stages of mitosis in order — remember PMAT: Prophase → Metaphase → Anaphase → Telophase.
Don't confuse continuous variation (a range, like height) with discontinuous variation (separate groups, like tongue rolling) — and remember that acquired variation (like a suntan) is NOT inherited.
Mitosis makes 2 identical cells with the same chromosome number (2n); meiosis makes 4 cells with half the number (n). This comparison is commonly tested.

interactiveLesson.instructions: Explore each labelled part of the DNA molecule. Select every hotspot to continue.

hotspots.label: Sugar-Phosphate Backbone
hotspots.fact: The two sides of the DNA ladder are made of alternating deoxyribose sugar and phosphate groups.

hotspots.label: Adenine (A)
hotspots.fact: Adenine is one of the four bases. It always pairs with Thymine (T).

hotspots.label: Thymine (T)
hotspots.fact: Thymine always pairs with Adenine, forming one rung of the ladder.

hotspots.label: Cytosine (C)
hotspots.fact: Cytosine is a base that always pairs with Guanine (G).

hotspots.label: Double Helix
hotspots.fact: The whole molecule twists into a double-helix shape, storing huge amounts of information compactly.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which of these is an example of continuous variation?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Height can take any value in a range, so it is continuous variation.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A suntan is best described as which type of variation?
practiceQuestions.explanation: A tan develops from sunlight during life, so it is acquired and not inherited.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Why does the polar bear have small ears?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Small ears have less surface area, so less body heat escapes.

practiceQuestions.prompt: What does a camel's hump store?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The hump stores fat as an energy reserve — not water.

practiceQuestions.prompt: What makes an adaptation different from an ordinary variation?

options: It gives a clear survival advantage

practiceQuestions.explanation: An adaptation is a variation that has been selected because it helps the organism survive.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Who founded the science of genetics?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Gregor Mendel founded genetics through his garden pea experiments.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A recessive allele is expressed only when:
practiceQuestions.explanation: A recessive trait shows only when two recessive alleles are present (no dominant allele).

practiceQuestions.prompt: In DNA, Adenine always pairs with:
practiceQuestions.explanation: A pairs with T, and C pairs with G.

practiceQuestions.prompt: How many daughter cells does mitosis produce?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Mitosis makes two genetically identical daughter cells.

practiceQuestions.prompt: What happens to the chromosome number during meiosis?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Meiosis halves the chromosome number to make gametes.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Gametes are haploid cells with half the chromosome number.
practiceQuestions.explanation: True — gametes are haploid (n); body cells are diploid (2n).

practiceQuestions.prompt: Acquired variation is passed on from parents to offspring.
practiceQuestions.explanation: False — acquired variation develops during life and is NOT inherited.

practiceQuestions.prompt: The twisted-ladder shape of a DNA molecule is called a double ______.
practiceQuestions.explanation: DNA's shape is a double helix.

practiceQuestions.prompt: During ______, the spindle forms and the chromosomes line up in the middle of the cell.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Metaphase is when chromosomes line up in the middle.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An organism with two identical alleles (BB or bb) is described as ______.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Two identical alleles = homozygous; two different = heterozygous.

sequencingActivity.prompt: Arrange the stages of the cell cycle in the correct order, starting before division.
sequencingActivity.explanation: A cell prepares and copies its DNA in Interphase, then divides through Prophase, Metaphase, Anaphase and Telophase (PMAT).

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: On an island, tortoises had different neck lengths. When only tall plants were left, long-necked tortoises survived and bred. After many generations all tortoises had long necks. This best illustrates:

options: A variation becoming an adaptation by natural selection

bossBattleQuestions.explanation: The long neck began as a variation and was selected over generations because it aided survival — becoming an adaptation through natural selection.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: A black-haired person carries one black allele (B, dominant) and one blond allele (b, recessive). Which statement is correct?

options: They are homozygous and will have blond children
They are heterozygous (Bb) and can pass on the blond allele

bossBattleQuestions.explanation: One dominant and one recessive allele is heterozygous (Bb); black hair shows, but the recessive blond allele can still be passed on.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: Why must meiosis halve the chromosome number when making gametes?

options: So that fertilisation restores the correct number (2n) in the offspring

bossBattleQuestions.explanation: If gametes were not halved, fusing two of them would double the chromosome number each generation. Halving keeps the species' number correct after fertilisation.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: Why do arctic animals tend to be large and round rather than small and thin?

options: Large round bodies have a smaller surface-area-to-volume ratio, so they lose less heat

bossBattleQuestions.explanation: A large, round shape has a smaller surface area for its volume, so less body heat is lost in the cold.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: How are mutations linked to evolution?

options: They always harm the organism and stop evolution
They are the original source of new variation, some of which natural selection can favour
They only affect body cells, never offspring
They replace the need for genes

bossBattleQuestions.explanation: Mutations create new alleles (new variation). If a mutation is beneficial and inherited, natural selection can spread it, driving evolution.
